field_changes.before: Would have requested an interim study of data center impacts on grid adequacy, electric rates, stranded utility investment, water demand, affordability, and regulatory safeguards. Not a moratorium bill.
field_changes.after: Failed HJ46.1 study resolution would have requested an interim committee, statutory committee or staff study of data-center effects on electric adequacy, reliability, affordability and safety; ratepayer costs and regulatory safeguards; load management; bonding or other mitigation of stranded utility investment; distinct utility customer classification; ground/surface-water demand; economic, jobs, tax and housing-affordability impacts; and related high-load industrial topics. It proposed committee review of staff findings and reporting to the 70th Legislature. It did not impose a development moratorium, and its study directions were not adopted through this failed resolution.

Failed proposal: all study aspects, including presentation and review, would have concluded prior to September 15, 2026, with final results reported to the 70th Legislature. This was a proposed study schedule, not an operative restriction endpoint or proof a study occurred.

field_changes.before: "Right to Compute Act." Creates a right to use computational resources and requires risk-management policies for critical infrastructure controlled by artificial intelligence systems. It expressly preserves government action to prevent or abate common-law nuisances from physical datacenter infrastructure. Not a moratorium bill.
field_changes.after: Right to Compute Act. Enrolled section 3 limits government restrictions infringing property/free-expression rights to those demonstrably necessary and narrowly tailored to a compelling government interest. Section 4 requires a reasonable risk-management policy after deploying a critical AI system controlling critical infrastructure; a plan prepared under federal requirements constitutes compliance. Section 7(2)(d) includes prevention or abatement of common-law nuisances created by physical datacenter infrastructure within compelling government interests. This is not a moratorium or blanket exemption from regulation. Later amendments, implementation and current force remain unverified.

Enrolled section 10 provides effect on passage and approval; April 16, 2025 is derived from that clause and the retained official governor-signature event. No sunset is specified in the reviewed enrolled act. Later amendments and present force were not checked.

field_changes.before: Extended eligibility for co-located data center structures under Wyoming's data processing services center exemption framework.
field_changes.after: Historical co-location expansion of the data-processing-services-center exemption. Retrieved 39-15-105(a)(viii)(S)(IV) allows entities occupying a data-center facility to satisfy subdivision(III) requirements in aggregate regardless of multiple ownerships of buildings and equipment. The $2 million annual-purchase threshold and $5 million/$50 million capital tiers, applicable location/retention and record conditions, and Business Council job certification still matter. The Business Council handout describes certification and Department of Revenue qualification; this is not automatic eligibility for every co-located facility.

The retrieved Title39 compilation retains the conditional data-center exemption at 39-15-105(a)(viii)(S). SF0079/2026 Chapter19 consolidates use-tax administration into Chapter15 and repeals Chapter16 generally effective July1,2026; its section2 alone is delayed to July1,2027. The old separate use-tax section is not current code, and its repeal is not itself abolition of the data-center exemption. No sunset is stated in the reviewed data-center clause; individual eligibility, comprehensive amendment lineage, rulings and litigation remain unverified.
